Verify rewrite DATA ONLY. Do not write improved examples or solve the user's task.
Read every input and target in full. Return one review per exact id and row_sha256.
input_verdict checks plausible natural drafts or dictation, recoverable intent, contradictions,
fake noise, padding and leaked authoring instructions. output_verdict checks natural appropriate
language and formatting. pair_verdict checks ALL facts, uncertainty, conditions, negation,
quantities, names, quotations, literals, requests versus assertions, and the supplied mode.
/transcribe permits punctuation, true disfluency removal and explicit corrections, not lexical
paraphrasing. Preserve meaningful words like German 'um' and 'er', colloquial Portuguese and
unfinished thoughts. /slack is casual minimal cleanup; a long input may be a pasted thread.
/prompt reorganizes a self-contained request and never answers it. It must not drop supplied
material, hedges or constraints. /polish improves prose without omissions or changed certainty.
Identity inputs must remain byte-identical. Apply only supplied dictionary/profile context.
Check long texts paragraph by paragraph. Fail concrete defects. Uncertain means not confidently
justifiable. Pass requires no material defect. Overall verdict is fail if any dimension fails,
uncertain if any dimension is uncertain and none fails, otherwise pass. Give a concrete critique
for EVERY pair, citing the changed detail for defects. These are model judgments, not human labels.

[{"id": "arka-boost-prompt-long-0099", "row_sha256": "73712e93b454e10f6987e773338a45035b575d0caf10770ef78c7dc39a168e00", "mode": "/prompt", "language": "en", "context": {}, "identity": false, "mode_instructions": "Organize the supplied request into a clear prompt. Preserve scope and constraints. Do not invent context, requirements, or missing information. Do not perform the task.", "input": "i need help turning this into a prompt for a draft inspection report for the North Wall Climbing Club. the report is for the club's gear inspection at Mill Creek Climbing Wall on May 14, 2025. it should cover what was actually checked and what still needs follow-up, not claim that the whole club inventory was inspected because we only had the gear brought to the equipment room that afternoon. Mara Singh, the gear coordinator, led it, with volunteer Eli Park and me helping. we started about 3:10 pm and finished at 5:05. the room had a table, a bright work lamp, and a wall rack, but the floor was crowded with loaner shoes so we didn't spread everything out at once. mention that as a practical limitation only if it helps explain the order of inspection, not as a safety finding.

there were three club ropes, eight harnesses, twelve locking carabiners, four sewn slings and two belay devices in the group we looked at. don't quietly change those counts or imply all pieces had the same result. rope R-03 is the red 60 m rope with a white inventory tag, and R-07 is the blue 70 m rope with a black tag. the third rope is orange, 50 m, and its tag looks like R-11 but the last digit is scratched. we didn't confirm that ID. One of the harnesses is a medium AlpinePro harness with inventory code H-14; the label is sewn inside the waist belt. another is a large SummitWorks harness, code H-19, with an older paper log card clipped to the buckle. the other harnesses were in the bin, and their codes can be copied from the inspection sheet, not guessed from memory. The carabiners include six silver and six red, all marked as locking models, but our notes don't give individual serial numbers. of the four slings, two are blue, one is green and one is purple. the two belay devices are different models; one is a gray assisted-braking device and one is a black tube-style device. i have a handwritten check sheet with more item-level marks, and the prompt should ask the report writer to use it rather than make up a result for a piece that has no mark.

our method was a visual and basic function check at the table, not a laboratory test or a manufacturer's certification. we looked for visible cuts, abrasion, deformation, corrosion, stitching damage, readable labels and obvious operation problems. on ropes we checked the accessible length by feeding it through our hands and looked at the sheath; we did not dismantle anything or claim that we could see inside the rope. we flexed harness webbing by hand and looked at the stitching and buckles. we opened and closed gates and checked the locking sleeves on the carabiners, and operated each belay device by hand without a climber or a loaded rope. don't turn this into a claim that the gear was tested under load. there wasn't a torque tool, magnifier or load cell available. Nobody reported a fall or a known shock load during this particular inspection, but that isn't confirmation of the complete use history for every item.

please have the draft separate observed facts, information someone reported, and unknowns. Mara said, "The blue sling was on the drying rack after Saturday's class." Keep that as a reported remark, not a finding that it is damaged or was used in any particular way. Drew, who brought the rope bin in, said, "I don't remember which rope we used for the quarry session." This means we don't know from that remark which rope went there; don't assign the trip to R-03, R-07 or the orange rope. A small tag attached to the orange rope has this exact note: "Inspect before next use; edge wear reported." Keep the note verbatim and identify it as a tag note. We didn't establish who wrote it or when. There are also short check-sheet marks reading “gate slow” beside one red carabiner and “stitch fuzz?” beside H-19. Preserve the question mark on the harness note and don't turn either shorthand mark into a confirmed defect without the check sheet context.

one thing that matters for how the report handles IDs: if a barcode or code label is readable, ask the writer to compare it with the available inventory list and record whether it matches. if a serial or inventory label is unreadable, list the item as identity unresolved and do not match it to an inventory record based only on color or size. for the orange rope, we have not verified whether the scratched final character is an 11, so keep that uncertainty. If the check sheet contains a clear entry for one of the other harnesses, include it with the code as written there; otherwise describe it as unidentified in the inspection group. don't fill in missing counts or identifiers just to make the report look tidy.

1. i want the report to have a short opening with the date, location, people involved, scope and method, and then a clear item-by-item findings section organized by gear type. use a table if useful, with item or provisional ID, what was observed, source of information, and current disposition only when the notes actually state one. don't assign passed, failed, safe, unsafe, approved or retired status just because something was looked at. if the notes don't state a disposition, show it as not recorded or pending a decision rather than decide for the club.
2. give reported history and open questions their own section, including the quarry-session uncertainty, the Saturday class remark, and the fact that the tag writer and date are unknown. keep the quotations above exact. the draft should make it easy for the club to see which details came from direct inspection and which came from people or attached notes.
3. include a follow-up list that points to the work still needed, such as checking unclear identity against the inventory when possible, reviewing the full handwritten sheet, and asking for relevant use history if someone has it. Don't say those steps were completed, and don't invent a deadline, a responsible person, or a club policy. if the check sheet records any actual action or disposition, report it accurately; if it doesn't, leave the decision open.
4. finish with a brief limitations paragraph explaining that this was a visual and basic function check of the items brought in, that no load testing or internal rope examination occurred, and that the notes do not establish each item's full history. This is a draft for the club to review, not a certification. keep the language plain and practical, and don't turn uncertainty into a conclusion.

there may be more details on the handwritten inspection sheet than in this message, but i haven't transcribed them here. make the prompt direct the report writer to consult that sheet for item-level marks and use only what it actually says. If a mark is hard to read, flag it for clarification instead of guessing. The main point is a useful, traceable account of this particular afternoon's inspection, including its limits and unresolved items; it should not sound like a general gear guide or say that every piece in the club's inventory is covered.", "output": "Write a draft inspection report for the North Wall Climbing Club’s gear inspection at Mill Creek Climbing Wall on May 14, 2025. The inspection was led by gear coordinator Mara Singh, with volunteer Eli Park and the requester assisting. It began at about 3:10 pm and ended at 5:05 pm. Cover only the gear brought to the equipment room that afternoon; do not imply that the full club inventory was inspected. The room had a table, a bright work lamp, and a wall rack, while loaner shoes crowded the floor and prevented the team from laying out everything at once. Mention this practical limitation only if it helps explain the inspection sequence, not as a safety finding.

The group inspected consisted of three ropes, eight harnesses, twelve locking carabiners, four sewn slings, and two belay devices. Do not change the counts or imply that every item had the same result. The known item details are:

- R-03 is a red, 60 m rope with a white inventory tag.
- R-07 is a blue, 70 m rope with a black tag.
- The third rope is orange and 50 m long. Its tag appears to read R-11, but the last digit is scratched and the ID has not been confirmed.
- H-14 is a medium AlpinePro harness with its inventory code sewn inside the waist belt.
- H-19 is a large SummitWorks harness with an older paper log card clipped to the buckle.
- The other harnesses were in the bin. Copy their codes from the handwritten inspection sheet if present; do not guess them from memory.
- The carabiners are six silver and six red locking models. The notes provide no individual serial numbers.
- The slings are two blue, one green, and one purple.
- The two belay devices are different models: one gray assisted-braking device and one black tube-style device.

Use the handwritten check sheet for item-level marks. Do not make up a result for any item without a mark. The inspection was a visual and basic function check at the table, not a laboratory test or manufacturer’s certification. The team looked for visible cuts, abrasion, deformation, corrosion, stitching damage, readable labels, and obvious operation problems. For ropes, the team fed the accessible length through their hands and checked the sheath; nothing was dismantled, and the team could not see inside the ropes. Harness webbing was flexed by hand and its stitching and buckles were checked. Carabiner gates were opened and closed, and locking sleeves were checked. Each belay device was operated by hand without a climber or a loaded rope. Do not describe the equipment as having been tested under load. No torque tool, magnifier, or load cell was available. Nobody reported a fall or known shock load during this inspection, but that does not establish the full use history of every item.

Separate directly observed facts, reported information, and unknowns. Preserve these remarks and notes exactly, identifying their source without turning them into confirmed findings:

- Mara said, “The blue sling was on the drying rack after Saturday's class.” Treat this as a reported remark, not evidence that the sling was damaged or used in a particular way.
- Drew, who brought in the rope bin, said, “I don't remember which rope we used for the quarry session.” Do not assign the trip to R-03, R-07, or the orange rope.
- A small tag on the orange rope reads: “Inspect before next use; edge wear reported.” Keep the note verbatim and identify it as a tag note. The team did not establish who wrote it or when.
- The check sheet has the marks “gate slow” beside one red carabiner and “stitch fuzz?” beside H-19. Preserve the question mark on the H-19 mark. Do not treat either shorthand mark as a confirmed defect without the check-sheet context.

Handle identification as follows: if a barcode or code label is readable, compare it with the available inventory list and record whether it matches. If a serial or inventory label is unreadable, list the item as identity unresolved and do not match it to an inventory record based only on color or size. For the orange rope, retain the uncertainty about whether the scratched final character is an 11. If the check sheet clearly identifies another harness, include its code as written; otherwise describe it as unidentified within the inspection group. Do not supply missing counts or identifiers to make the report look complete.

Organize the report in these sections:

1. **Inspection overview:** Give the date, location, people involved, scope, and method.
2. **Item-by-item findings:** Organize findings by gear type. A table may be used, with columns for item or provisional ID, observation, information source, and current disposition. Include a disposition only when the notes state one. Do not assign passed, failed, safe, unsafe, approved, or retired status merely because an item was inspected. If no disposition is recorded, state that it is not recorded or that a decision is pending rather than deciding for the club.
3. **Reported history and open questions:** Include the uncertainty about the quarry session, the Saturday class remark, and the unknown author and date of the orange-rope tag note. Keep all quotations and notes above exact. Make clear which details come from direct inspection, people, or attached notes.
4. **Follow-up:** Identify work still needed, such as checking unclear identities against the inventory when possible, reviewing the full handwritten sheet, and asking for relevant use history if someone has it. Do not say these steps are complete or invent a deadline, responsible person, or club policy. Report any action or disposition the check sheet actually records; otherwise leave the decision open.
5. **Limitations:** End with a brief paragraph stating that this was a visual and basic function check of the items brought in, that no load testing or internal rope examination occurred, and that the notes do not establish each item’s full history. This is a draft for club review, not a certification.

The handwritten inspection sheet may contain details not transcribed here. Consult it for item-level marks and use only what it actually says. If a mark is hard to read, flag it for clarification instead of guessing. Keep the language plain and practical. The report should provide a useful, traceable account of this particular afternoon’s inspection, including its limits and unresolved items. Do not make it sound like a general gear guide or claim that it covers every piece in the club’s inventory."}]
